meta.name: CompTIA Data+ (DA0-001)
meta.notes: Initial seed pack covering the five DA0-001 domains: data concepts and environments, data mining, data analysis, visualization, and data governance/quality.

questions.question: Your team needs to ingest customer-support email bodies, JPEG screenshots, and voicemail WAV files into a single analytical store. How should this content be classified?
options: Structured data (rows and columns with a defined schema)
Semi-structured data (self-describing tags but no fixed schema)
Streaming data (continuous time-ordered events)
Unstructured data (no predefined model or schema)
questions.explanation: Email bodies, images and audio files do not fit a tabular schema and contain no self-describing markers, so they are unstructured data. Structured data is row/column with a fixed schema (relational tables, CSV). Semi-structured data has self-describing tags or keys (JSON, XML) but no rigid schema. Streaming refers to the delivery cadence, not the shape of the payload, so a batch upload of WAV files is still unstructured regardless of how it is transported.

questions.question: A retailer needs a system that records thousands of small concurrent point-of-sale transactions per second with strong ACID guarantees on inserts and updates. Which workload pattern fits best?
options: OLAP (column-oriented warehouse tuned for ad-hoc analytical queries)
OLTP (row-oriented database tuned for short transactional writes)
Data lake (raw object storage for unstructured exploration)
ETL pipeline (batch movement of data between stores)
questions.explanation: OLTP (online transaction processing) systems are row-oriented relational databases optimized for high-concurrency, low-latency inserts/updates with full ACID guarantees — exactly the POS use case. OLAP is built for large analytical scans, not transactional writes. A data lake is unmanaged object storage with no ACID semantics on individual rows. ETL is a movement pattern, not a workload type, and would not service live POS writes.

questions.question: An analytics team copies raw event logs from S3 into Snowflake first, then runs transformations using Snowflake's SQL engine on the loaded data. Which integration pattern are they using?
options: ETL (extract → transform → load)
CDC (change data capture only)
Reverse ETL (warehouse → operational systems)
ELT (extract → load → transform)
questions.explanation: Loading raw data into the warehouse first and then transforming it inside the warehouse engine is the defining shape of ELT. Classic ETL transforms data in an intermediate engine before loading. CDC describes how source changes are detected, not where the transform runs. Reverse ETL moves data from the warehouse out to operational systems (CRM, ad platforms) and is the opposite direction.

questions.question: A team must collect real-time stock-trade events with millisecond latency to feed a fraud-detection model. Which acquisition method best fits the requirement?
options: Streaming ingestion via a message bus (Kafka or Kinesis)
Flat-file batch export every night
Web scraping the broker's website hourly
Manual entry into a spreadsheet
questions.explanation: Millisecond-latency ingestion is the textbook case for a streaming message bus such as Kafka or Kinesis, where producers publish events and consumers process them continuously. Nightly batch files arrive hours late, hourly web scraping is even slower and brittle, and manual spreadsheet entry cannot scale to event rates at all — none can meet a real-time fraud SLA.

questions.question: A marketing analyst reports last quarter's revenue, average order value, and churn rate to summarize what already happened in the business. Which type of analytics is this?
options: Descriptive analytics (what happened)
Diagnostic analytics (why it happened)
Predictive analytics (what is likely to happen next)
Prescriptive analytics (what action to take)
questions.explanation: Summarizing past KPIs to show what happened is the definition of descriptive analytics. Diagnostic analytics goes a step further to explain why a KPI moved (root-cause, drill-down). Predictive analytics forecasts future values using statistical or ML models. Prescriptive analytics recommends an action (next-best offer, optimization) and is the most advanced of the four.

questions.question: An exam-score distribution is heavily right-skewed by a small group of very high scores. Which measure of central tendency best represents the typical student?
options: Mean (sum divided by count)
Median (middle value of an ordered set)
Mode (most frequently occurring value)
Range (maximum minus minimum)
questions.explanation: In a skewed distribution the mean is pulled toward the long tail and overstates the typical case, so the median — the value that splits the ordered data in half — is the more representative center. The mode reports the most common bucket but ignores the rest of the distribution and can be misleading when ties exist. Range is a spread statistic, not a center, and does not describe a typical student at all.

questions.question: A chart shows that monthly ice-cream sales and drowning incidents both peak in July. What is the most defensible interpretation?
options: Ice-cream sales cause drownings
Drownings cause ice-cream sales
Both variables rise with summer weather, which acts as a confounder
The chart proves there is no relationship between the variables
questions.explanation: When two variables move together, the safest conclusion is correlation with a likely confounder — here, warm weather drives both ice-cream consumption and swimming exposure. Asserting either direction of causation from a co-movement is the classic correlation-vs-causation fallacy. Claiming "no relationship" contradicts the visible joint peak; there is a relationship, it is just not a direct causal one.

questions.question: An executive wants to compare quarterly revenue across five product lines over the last four years. Which visualization is most appropriate?
options: Line chart with one series per product line over time
Pie chart per quarter showing proportions of one whole
Single histogram of all revenue values
Treemap of total four-year revenue per product
questions.explanation: Comparing trends over time across a handful of categories is the canonical use case for a multi-series line chart — the x-axis carries time and each product line is its own line. Pie charts only show part-to-whole at one moment and break down with many slices and many quarters. A histogram shows the distribution of a single variable, not change over time. A treemap collapses time entirely and only shows static proportions.

questions.question: Which visualization is best for showing average response time across days of the week and hours of the day in a single chart?
options: Scatter plot of response time versus time of day
Stacked bar chart with one bar per day
Heatmap with day and hour on the two axes and color-encoded values
Doughnut chart of total response time per day
questions.explanation: A heatmap encodes a numeric value with color over two categorical or binned axes, making it the natural choice for a day × hour grid where you want to spot patterns at a glance. A scatter plot would overplot and lose the day axis. A stacked bar can show daily totals but cannot resolve the 24 hourly buckets compactly. A doughnut collapses the hourly dimension entirely and only shows part-to-whole per day.

questions.question: A new analyst is granted access to a table containing customer names, email addresses, and Social Security numbers. According to common data-classification practice, this dataset should be labeled as:
options: Public (no restriction on disclosure)
Internal-only (low sensitivity within the company)
Anonymous aggregate data
Confidential PII (regulated personally identifiable information)
questions.explanation: A combination of name, email and SSN is directly identifying and is regulated under privacy laws, so it must be classified at the most restrictive tier — typically labeled Confidential PII (or Restricted) with mandatory access controls and audit logging. Public is reserved for data safe to disclose externally. Internal-only is for low-sensitivity business data with no privacy or regulatory exposure. The dataset is not anonymized — every row identifies a specific person — so the "anonymous aggregate" label would itself be a control failure.

questions.question: A single customer is represented by one row in the CRM, the billing system, and the support tool. The customer's identifier is the same in all three rows, but the spelling of their name differs slightly across the systems. Which data-quality dimension is MOST directly violated?
options: Timeliness (data freshness)
Consistency (same values across systems for the same entity)
Validity (conformance to a defined format or rule)
Uniqueness (one record per real-world entity within a system)
questions.explanation: When the same identified entity carries different attribute values across systems, the failing dimension is consistency — the systems disagree on the truth. Timeliness concerns how current a value is, not whether systems agree. Validity asks whether each value satisfies a rule or pattern (an email must contain an @), which can pass even when the systems disagree with each other. Uniqueness would fire if the same person had multiple rows within one system; the question says each system holds exactly one row.

questions.question: You need a report listing every product, including products that have not yet had any sales, alongside their sales totals when those exist. Which SQL JOIN type produces this result when starting from the products table?
options: INNER JOIN (returns only rows with matches in both tables)
RIGHT OUTER JOIN from products to sales
LEFT OUTER JOIN from products to sales
CROSS JOIN (Cartesian product of both tables)
questions.explanation: A LEFT OUTER JOIN keeps every row from the left table (products) and fills NULL for the sales columns when no matching sales row exists — exactly the "every product, with sales when available" semantic. INNER JOIN drops products with no sales, defeating the requirement. RIGHT OUTER JOIN would instead keep every sale and could miss product rows that have no sales. CROSS JOIN pairs every product with every sale and produces a meaningless explosion of rows.
